opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. If I had to pick one thing, I'd say it's the data problem, and it's different from the data problem in language or vision.

In consumer AI you can scrape the internet and get trillions of tokens. In science, high-quality data is scarce, expensive, and often locked inside individual labs. A single protein structure, a reliable materials measurement, or a well-controlled reaction outcome can take weeks of experimental work. And much of what exists is biased. Journals publish successes, so our datasets are full of reactions that worked and molecules that bound, and they rarely include the failures that a model actually needs to learn where the boundaries are.

The second layer is that scientific data is multi-scale and multimodal in a way that's hard to unify. You might have quantum-level simulations, crystallography, spectroscopy, cell imaging, and clinical outcomes all describing the same underlying system, but at completely different resolutions and with different noise characteristics. Building representations that respect the physics across those scales, rather than just pattern-matching within one, is still very much an open problem.

Third is validation. In language, a human can glance at an output and judge it. In science, the model proposes a new catalyst or drug candidate, and the only real test is going back to the wet lab or running an expensive simulation. So the feedback loop is slow, and that makes iterating on models much harder than in other domains.

That's why I think the most important progress will come from closing the loop: pairing models with automated or high-throughput experimentation, so AI designs the experiment, the lab runs it, and the results, including the negative ones, flow straight back into training. Whoever builds that data flywheel well, in a specific domain, will have a real advantage, more than whoever has the cleverest architecture.

r001.rationale: The response says scientific proposals must be tested in a wet lab or expensive simulation and that this slow feedback loop makes iteration difficult.

r002.rationale: It advocates automated or high-throughput experiments whose results flow straight back into training, connecting rapid experimental data production with ongoing model training.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that resolving experimental verification would still leave open whether AI can generate hypotheses beyond existing knowledge.

r004.rationale: It does not claim that inability to generate new hypotheses limits an iterative AI-driven scientific search.

r005.rationale: It does not identify generating ideas that are both scientifically innovative and feasible as an unresolved challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the hardest part isn't the models themselves, it's the data, and more specifically, the gap between what the physical world gives you and what a learning system needs.

In language or vision, the data is essentially free. Humans have been writing and taking pictures for decades, and it's all sitting there. In science, every data point costs something real. A materials synthesis run might take a week. A protein measurement might take months and a grad student's sanity. So you're working in a regime where you have maybe a few thousand labeled examples, and they're noisy, biased toward whatever was easy or fashionable to measure, and often reported without the failures. Nobody publishes the ninety-nine samples that didn't superconduct.

So the technical question becomes: how do you build systems that learn efficiently from scarce, expensive, biased data, and how do you close the loop so the model decides what experiment to run next? That's where I think the real frontier is. It's not training a bigger transformer on arXiv. It's integrating prediction, uncertainty, and physical priors into something that can say, "I don't know this region well, go measure here," and then actually have a lab, robotic or human, act on it. Active learning sounds simple on a slide, but making it robust when every query costs a thousand dollars and a week is genuinely hard.

The second piece, which is related, is that physics doesn't care about your loss function. The model has to respect conservation laws, symmetries, the fact that a crystal structure has to be stable. If you just pattern-match, you get beautiful predictions that violate thermodynamics. Encoding that structure without crippling the model's flexibility is an unsolved problem, and honestly I think it's where someone with both a physics background and an ML background can contribute most right now.

r001.rationale: The response calls scarce, costly scientific data the main challenge and discusses running experiments to acquire it, but does not identify physical experiments as a verification bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It describes experiments as slow and data as scarce; it does not connect rapid experimental data production to frequent model post-training.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss whether AI can generate scientific hypotheses beyond existing knowledge.

r004.rationale: It does not say that limited hypothesis generation constrains iterative AI-driven scientific search.

r005.rationale: It discusses learning from data and respecting physical laws, but not the unresolved challenge of generating ideas that are both innovative and feasible.

astra-6.text:
I think the hardest challenge is bridging the gap between finding patterns and discovering something scientifically meaningful. A model can fit the data very well, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it has learned the underlying physics or can predict what happens outside the conditions it was trained on.

In science, that distinction is crucial. Often, the regime we care most about is precisely the one where we have very little data. So how do we incorporate physical constraints, quantify uncertainty, and make predictions that survive an experimental test? To me, that’s the central technical challenge: connecting a model’s predictions to a reliable process of scientific validation.

r001.rationale: It calls connecting predictions to reliable scientific validation the central technical challenge and asks whether predictions survive an experimental test.

r002.rationale: It does not connect rapid production of experimental data with frequent model post-training.

r003.rationale: It does not say that resolving experimental verification would still leave AI unable to generate hypotheses beyond existing knowledge.

r004.rationale: It does not describe how inability to generate new hypotheses limits iterative AI-driven scientific search.

r005.rationale: It discusses scientific meaning and validation, but does not identify generating ideas that are both innovative and feasible as an unresolved challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hardest challenge is connecting what a model learns from data with the underlying mechanisms of a scientific problem. A model can be very good at prediction, but in science we often need more: we want to know why something happens, whether the result respects physical constraints, and whether it will hold under conditions we haven’t measured before.

That becomes especially difficult when data is scarce or expensive to collect. So the question is how to combine learning with existing scientific knowledge—and then design experiments that can genuinely test the model’s predictions. To me, that loop between prediction and experimental validation is the core technical challenge.

r001.rationale: The response calls experimental validation a core challenge, but does not specify verification through physical experiments.

r002.rationale: It mentions scarce data, but not rapid production of physical data or frequent model post-training.

r003.rationale: It does not say that solving verification would still leave AI’s ability to generate beyond-knowledge hypotheses unestablished.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss how limited hypothesis generation constrains iterative AI-driven scientific search.

r005.rationale: It does not identify generating ideas that are both scientifically innovative and feasible as an unresolved challenge.
